To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) an increase in central venous pressure due to water immersion is accompanied by a suppression of the plasma arginine vaspressin concentration; (2) the plasma arginine vassopressin concentration is suppressed during water immersion in the neck-deep position, despite an increase in plasma osmolalitiy, and a marked osmotic diuresi; (3) the plasma argine vasopressin concentration was suppressed during water immersion despite an increase in systolic arterial pressure
an increase in central venous pressure is associated with a reduction in plasma arginine vasoppresin in healthy subjects.

1) an increase in central venous pressure due to water immersion is accompanied by suppressed arginine vasoppressin release in man; 2) this suppression of arginine vasotressin release is not due to changes in plasma osmolalilty or arterial pressure; 3) the suppression of arginine-vasopressin release may contribute to the natriuresis observed in water immersion; and 4) the suppression of vasopressin release is a specific response
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of central venous pressure on plasma arginine vasotocin and plasma osmolality during immersion in man.
the influence of increased central blood volume (CBV) due to immersion on plasma arginine vasotressin (AVP), plasma volume and fluid balance in humans.
the influence of increased centralvenous pressure (C VP ) on the plasma concentration ( pAVP ) ofarginine vasopressin( AVP ).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
an increase in plasma volume and/or an increase in CYP is not a stimulus to AVP secretion.
the increase in CVP during WI is accompanied by a suppressed pAVP and a pronounced natriuresis, and thus the increase in plasma volume is counteracted.
a high CVP, which is associated with an increased intrathoracic pressure, inhibits the secretion of AVP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the increased CVP during WI suppresses pAVP and thus the release of ADH, which in turn leads to the observed natriuresis.
the increase in CVP is not sufficient to stimulate AVP release.
the increased central venous volume during water immersion leads to a decrease in plasma AVP.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the increase of CVP is associated with a reduction in plasma arginine vasotocin (pAVT).
the increase in CVP is not a direct stimulus for vasopressin release in humans.
the CVP is a good indicator of the fluid status of the body.
